label: Nationality discrimination in access to employment
priority_reason: A key recommendation on non-discrimination against EU workers is repeated in the 2020 to 2025 reports, and equal access is central to the chapter. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found in the evidence.
tractability_reason: The change is legal and within the government's control, and the same law was amended in 2021 and 2025. Against that, six reports record no alignment and the requirement runs to the time of accession, so there is no evidence of past progress.
direction_reason: Sub-area wording on access to the labour market, which matches this issue, says no progress in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, and the 2025 report says there were no legislative developments. The 2025 screening finding of partial alignment is a first assessment of that kind and does not show a change.
gap_reason: What remains is equal treatment of EU workers in the law on access to the labour market, including an end to posts in private companies reserved for nationals. The foreigners law is itself the barrier, the 2025 amendment only renames bodies and the further amendments are only proposed with unknown content (all statuses are proposals; the two government items are machine translated, so capped at Medium), while the country's general ban on nationality discrimination is its own account and does not close the gap. The Commission's statement that the law makes no EU distinction conflicts with the country's account on quotas, which is reported and partly explained under RI-FMW-002.

Permit counts (755 in 2021, some 8 900 in 2024) are not used as a trend, because the bases appear to differ: the 2021 figure sits beside 3 242 separate opinions in a machine-translated agency report, capped at Medium.
gap_reason: What remains is access for EU citizens without work permits or residence permits, with their explicit exclusion from quotas, and no responding intervention is linked (statuses are proposals). The confirmed contradiction stands: the Commission says the law does not distinguish EU citizens, while the country says quotas do not apply to them under a reciprocity agreement. Art. 5(2) point 1 of the 2015 law (machine translated, so capped at Medium, and used under LIM-0024) partly explains this, because it does exempt foreigners given equality under such an agreement, but it is conditional, no item identifies a concluded agreement or shows it applied, and the Commission still requires the exclusion.

What remains is independence shown in appointments and practice, more competition in a concentrated mobile market, and resolving the financing provisions for the Operational and Technical Agency, on which the Commission and the country disagree and which concern that agency and not the regulator itself.

label: Broadband and high-capacity network coverage uneven

Delivery therefore needs the ministry, the public broadcasting enterprise, operators and outside funders.

National averages did rise, with home internet access at 90.8% in 2024, 5G coverage at 76% in 2023 and 97% in a machine-translated 2025 national source, and some progress on ICT infrastructure in matching sub-area wording in 2025, while differences between earlier household figures reflect different measures, not conflict. No series tracks the rural and small-business gap itself, so the averages do not show that the unevenness has narrowed, and the chapter scale was not decisive.
gap_reason: Latest EU items still ask for more access for smaller companies and rural areas, while the compared statuses, which are proposals for G6, show 5G roll-out in practice but the national optical network only proposed. Sources conflict on the size of the gap: the ICT strategy gives 77% fixed coverage against an EU average of 78%, the Commission gives 79.6% against 93.1%, and the strategy elsewhere gives 77% as very high capacity coverage after stating 69%, so the comparison with the EU cannot be relied on until the measures are checked. What remains is fixed broadband for small firms and rural areas, very low take-up of the fastest connections, and completing the 5G roll-out named in the Reform Agenda.

label: Broadband planning and investment framework incomplete
priority_reason: The requirement is repeated by the EU, in the 2022 and 2023 assessments and the 2025 screening, but it is not named in a benchmark, a Reform Agenda payment step or the chapter's key recommendations. The Reform Agenda plan does call the broadband network the most important digital project, but as an investment, so the issue matters for the theme with thinner support than the legal and regulator issues.
tractability_reason: Updating targets is within the government's control and a mapping study is the stated first step, but financing the network depends on outside funders, State aid alignment and a public enterprise whose capacity the Commission says needs strengthening. Past progress is weak: the plan was delayed in 2021 and 2022, and the national broadband competence office, reported in machine translation, finds none of three measures implemented. The financing figures come from a table flagged as possibly misread, so they support only the general point that funding is mixed.
direction_reason: The plan's implementation slowed in 2021 and was further delayed in 2022, a strategic approach to broadband was found lacking in 2022 and 2023, the plan was said only to remain valid in 2024 and 2025, and the 2025 screening asks for its targets to be aligned with the Digital Decade; the 2020 chapter-wide some progress is context and was not decisive. Newer Reform Agenda investment and a feasibility study are plans and do not yet show change, so this is not improving, and no 2026 Commission item addresses the framework. Sources conflict on the plan's period, with ITU and the 2025 report giving 2019-2029 and the 2022 and 2024 reports giving 2019-2023, which affects how far the delays can be measured against targets.
gap_reason: The latest EU items ask for targets aligned with the Digital Decade, further alignment on aid for broadband and stronger capacity at the public broadcasting enterprise. The compared statuses are proposals for G6: the ICT strategy with its 2030 goals is adopted, but its alignment with the Digital Decade is the government's own statement in machine translation, and target alignment, State aid and the national network are only proposed, while none of the three plan measures towards the 100 Mbps target has been implemented. What remains is updating the plan's targets, settling the aid rules and financing the backhaul network; the reported non-use of the Western Balkans Investment Framework for infrastructure sits beside technical assistance from it for a feasibility study, which appears to be a difference between study and construction but should be checked.

label: Base registers incomplete, unreliable or not digitalised
priority_reason: The Commission's main findings gave the same key recommendation to complete register digitalisation in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and base registers are central to the digital government theme. The recommendation is one clause of a wider one on administrative procedures and is shared with the data exchange and e-services issues, which reviewers may weigh. The Reform Agenda payment step on a register of charges is flagged as doubtful for this theme and was not relied on.
tractability_reason: The operating population register shows that delivery is possible, and a register platform was begun with EU support. Against that, completion needs many institutions and municipalities to act, and the strategy's baseline of no digital registers in 2022 shows how much remains. The two strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.
direction_reason: The Commission repeated the need to improve population register data in 2021, 2022 and 2023, and the same recommendation to complete the digitalisation of institutions' registers in 2023, 2024 and 2025, with use of the register still limited in 2024. The 2025 mention of efforts does not change the recommendation, so the default of persistent applies. The Chapter 10 scale is context only and was not decisive.
gap_reason: The population register is proposed as in practice, but the register platform, the Register of Registers and the wider e-services reform are all proposed only, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is to complete the digitalisation of institutional, municipal property and intellectual property registers and to raise the quality and use of population register data. The fully digital National Real Estate Register and the Commission's analogue property registers are a noted difference of register and level, not a conflict, and the machine-translated strategy on low use is capped at Medium confidence.

label: Open data and re-use of public sector information incomplete
priority_reason: The Commission raises the matter in 2020, 2022 and 2025, but not in its main findings, so it is a repeated requirement that is not central. Most items here come from one national audit and one national strategy, and that volume was not treated as importance.
tractability_reason: One ministry leads, the portal and 74 publishing institutions already existed by 2022, and the stated cause of the outage is a procurement problem rather than a structural one. Progress does not depend on the EU, although the amendments have been slow since 2023. This view leans on machine-translated items capped at Medium confidence, and government reporting on datasets does not itself show success.
direction_reason: Commission items ask for regular data updates in 2020 and more proactive disclosure in 2022, while amendments for Open Data Directive alignment were in preparation in 2023 and still with a working group in 2025; the 2020 sub-area rating of some progress concerns transparency more widely and, like the chapter scale, was not decisive. The State Audit Office reports that the portal has not functioned since early 2025, in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and the country's published screening presentation describes the portal favourably without addressing this. That outage rests on one source with no later status, so it does not yet support worsening, though confirmation would.
gap_reason: A Law on the Use of Public Sector Data is adopted and 580 datasets were reported by 2022, but the amendments and the Directive alignment action are proposed only, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is alignment with the Open Data Directive and regular publication by institutions on a functioning portal. Sources conflict, since the October 2025 strategy says the country is not aligned while the screening report's country presentation says partially aligned, so both are the country's own statements (the conflict register attributes the second to the Commission), and the Commission's own finding is only that further efforts are needed; the machine-translated items are capped at Medium confidence.

label: Personal data protection law not aligned with EU rules
priority_reason: Full alignment is a recommendation repeated in the Commission's 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and the 2024 and 2025 main findings record no progress on personal data protection. The legal framework is central to the data theme and to fundamental rights under Chapter 23.
tractability_reason: Texts already exist: the Agency drafted amendments in April 2022 and a Law Enforcement Directive draft reached Parliament with, as the Agency reports, a positive informal Commission opinion. Yet the Government withdrew that draft in 2022, neither process moved in 2025, and sector laws need several ministries. The Agency's annual report items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.
direction_reason: The Commission found no concrete progress on the Law Enforcement Directive in 2020, partial alignment and a need for full alignment in 2023, and pending alignment in 2024 and 2025, so the requirement has not changed across three or more reports. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2024 and 2025 covers more than this issue and was not decisive. The 2025 transfer amendment without equivalent safeguards is a further concern but a single event.
gap_reason: The 2020 law is proposed as in practice, with the Commission confirming full application from August 2021, while the amendments and the Law Enforcement Directive law are proposed only, the earlier draft was withdrawn in 2022, and all these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is full alignment with the General Data Protection Regulation, a law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, safeguards for transfers, harmonised sector laws and confirmed ePrivacy alignment. Sources conflict, since the State Audit Office and the Agency's strategy describe the law as aligned while the Commission calls the framework insufficient, and the country claims full ePrivacy alignment while the Commission seeks further efforts; this judgement does not rely on Article 122 of the unofficial translation (MKD-GOV-2020-001-0043), which may be mistranslated and, read literally, would suspend core chapters until accession.

label: Data protection authority lacks independence and resources
priority_reason: The Commission raised the Agency's dependence or capacity in every report from 2021 to 2025, named its independence as an area requiring alignment in 2023, and recommended stronger capacity in 2025. An independent, resourced authority is central to the data theme, and other data protection issues depend on it.
tractability_reason: Only a few domestic actors are needed, a draft has existed since April 2022 and the budget is small. Past progress is poor, however: the draft has not moved, the Ministry of Finance repeatedly refused funds or returned the employment plan, and the director post took most of 2025 to fill. The Agency's reports are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and they are a party's account of its own constraints.
direction_reason: The Commission moved from dependence on ministries in 2021 and understaffing in 2022 and 2023 to staff falling further in 2024 and no director in 2025, with reported staff of 21, then 20, then 18 at the end of 2024 and 17 at the end of 2025. The last two counts are the Agency's own, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, but they run the same way as the Commission's findings. The Agency reports a director from 5 December 2025, which is a later date than the Commission's finding, not a conflict, and the chapter scale was not decisive.
gap_reason: The amendments meant to secure the Agency's autonomy are proposed only, and the 2025-2030 strategy's proposed status of implemented means only that work has begun, with the Commission finding it was held back; these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is autonomy in hiring and spending, and funding and staff that match the Agency's tasks. Statements that the Agency is independent describe its legal status, while the Commission and the Agency's own reports describe its operating dependence, so this is a noted difference and not a conflict.

label: Data protection authority not consulted and its advice not followed
priority_reason: The finding recurs in every report from 2020 to 2025 and the Commission called the 2025 removal concerning, but the 2023 list of areas requiring alignment does not include it and it is not in the main findings. It is a repeated requirement that supports the authority's role rather than being central to the theme, and reviewers may weigh the 2025 reversal differently.
tractability_reason: Restoring the consultation duty is a change to the Government's own Rules of Procedure, which the Agency identifies precisely and which depends on no one outside the country. Getting ministries to follow advice and Parliament to act on reports is harder, and the Government removed the duty recently. The Agency's items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.
direction_reason: The Commission's finding was essentially unchanged from 2020 to 2024, with some progress noted in 2021, and then changed in 2025, when the Government removed the Agency from the mandatory consultation list and Parliament amended the law without consulting it. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2025 matches this issue and the chapter scale was not decisive. The Agency's report confirms the deletion in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and its count of opinions (5 for 2024, 15 for 2025) does not show that consultation improved.
gap_reason: No intervention is recorded as responding to this issue, and the one recent measure, the removal from the consultation list, has a proposed status of implemented and runs the opposite way; these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is systematic consultation of the Agency on sector and implementing laws, follow-up of its recommendations and follow-up of its reports in Parliament.

label: Weak compliance with data protection rules
priority_reason: Compliance is central to whether the law has effect, but the Commission's direct findings on it are thin, mainly 2023 and 2025, and it is not a named key recommendation. The large volume of items comes from the Agency's own reports and was not treated as importance.
tractability_reason: Progress needs behaviour to change across very many public and private controllers, and it depends on an Agency whose supervision and misdemeanour capacity is shrinking. The evidence shows awareness work and enforcement activity, but no sustained improvement in compliance. The Agency's items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.
direction_reason: The Commission called fines low in 2020, found in general that controllers do not implement the law in 2023, and in 2025 found low awareness and more frequent breaches, some unreported; the 2022 statement of progress on compliance sits in the paragraph on one body's supervision, so it is not a general trend. The Agency's statements of significant progress concern its own application of the framework, a noted difference from the Commission's sub-area rating, and supervision counts measure enforcement rather than compliance. The chapter scale was not decisive, and the machine-translated Agency findings are capped at Medium confidence.
gap_reason: The security rulebook has been adopted and the e-classroom is proposed as implemented, but the data protection officer network and the sanction amendments are proposed only, no independent evidence shows changed behaviour, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is for controllers, including public bodies, to apply the law, report breaches and face effective sanctions. Reprimand counts conflict between the Commission's report (10 for 2022, 17 for 2021) and the country presentation (4 for each), and low notification numbers (19 for 2022, 11 for 2025) are read by the Agency as under-reporting, so they do not conflict with the Commission's finding of more frequent breaches.

label: Personal data protection in electoral processes weak
priority_reason: The Commission raised it only in 2022 and 2023, it is not in the main findings, and it is peripheral to the data theme.
tractability_reason: Few actors are needed and an assessment of the Code is a limited task, and the State Election Commission has already acted on some irregularities. Oversight of campaign data and any change to the Electoral Code are likely to be harder, and the evidence on this is thin.
direction_reason: The Commission used the same wording in three documents, its 2022 and 2023 reports and the 2023 screening report, but no item after 2023 addresses the issue, so the record shows neither that it continues nor that it has eased. The three-report default for persistent was therefore not applied, because the repeats span only two years and the 2024 and 2025 reports are silent. The chapter scale was not decisive.
gap_reason: The latest requirement, from 2023, is unmet on the record: no intervention is recorded as responding and the Electoral Code's biometric provisions have a proposed status of adopted, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is an assessment of the Code against data protection law and proper oversight of personal data used in campaigns. The State Election Commission addressed some irregularities, but that does not reach these two points, and this finding rests on evidence no newer than 2023.

label: Cybersecurity legal and strategic framework incomplete
priority_reason: The law and strategy, an operational competent authority and the NIS2 frameworks are each Reform Agenda payment steps, and NIS2 or cybersecurity legislation recurs in the Commission's key recommendations from 2022 to 2025. The issue is the legal base on which the rest of the cybersecurity theme rests. The rating rests on these EU requirements and not on the large number of national plan and audit items.
tractability_reason: Much of what remains is drafting that the Ministry controls, and adoption followed within a year of the Reform Agenda step, which favours progress; against this, the first draft law stalled from 2019 to 2025, the Council barely functioned and no item shows the by-laws adopted after their deadline. Coordination needs many bodies, the strategy itself names political support and budget as key risks, and one reporting obligation to ENISA cannot be met outside the EU. Tractability is therefore higher for legal alignment than for coordination.
direction_reason: Commission items moved from no further progress on the 2019 draft law in 2021, through repeated calls to adopt the law and strategy in 2022, 2023 and 2024, to adoption of the strategy in January 2025 and the law in June 2025, which the 2025 report counts as some progress. The chapter scale (limited progress 2021 to 2024, some progress 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and the improvement lies in the legal and strategic framework, since no item shows better coordination after the 2023 call, the 2024 audit finding of a Council that met once and the 2025 strategy's own description of coordination as critical. A February 2022 ITU item lists the law as existing while the Commission's 2022 report says it was still a draft, and later Commission and audit items support the draft reading; the differing dates for the Council (2019 or 2020) and the action plan's end (2027 or 2028) do not affect this value.
gap_reason: The Commission found the 2025 law sufficient for the Reform Agenda step, which required alignment of primary legislation only, yet says it does not fully align with the acquis and still asks the country to continue aligning; the law, strategy and competent authority are proposed as adopted and the by-laws and disclosure and crisis frameworks as proposed, and these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is the outstanding NIS2 provisions and Cybersecurity Act certification alignment (last raised before the law passed), the 15 by-laws legally due within six months but not shown as adopted, the entity lists, the disclosure and crisis frameworks, working coordination, and application to the sectors the law defers until accession. The law's text is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and the regulator's one-line statement that the strategy is applied is government reporting without specifics, so neither is treated as closure.

label: Operational cybersecurity capacity of public institutions weak
priority_reason: Operational national and government CERTs, a staffed competent authority and a secure government network are Reform Agenda payment steps, and the Commission has repeated the need for capacity in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports. The Commission's reform programme assessments also name these deficiencies, and without operating capacity the legal framework has little effect, so the issue is central to the theme. The rating does not rest on the volume of audit and action plan items.
tractability_reason: Progress needs people the state has struggled to hire and keep (IT posts about half filled, 3 of 11 MKD-CIRT posts filled, a shortage the strategy says extends across the region), action across about 140 bodies, and budgets the strategy itself calls at risk, while the main infrastructure is at pre-feasibility stage and looks to outside funding. Past progress is weak, as most surveyed institutions had no response team five years after the previous strategy called for them, and the new 40% salary supplement is adopted with no item yet showing its effect. Strengthening MKD-CIRT alone would be more achievable than system-wide capacity, and the audit and strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.
direction_reason: The Commission's wording is essentially unchanged across three reports, that state institutions need stronger capacity and infrastructure and the national centre more staff (2023, 2024, 2025), and its reform programme assessments repeat large or major deficiencies in 2025 and 2026, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Incident counts cannot show a trend in capacity, because reporting was not mandatory and the figures are not comparable (1,441 or 1,443 for 2020, 2,804 for 2022, about 170 in 2023 on an unstated definition). The World Bank's advanced rating and the audit's finding of poor protection are a noted difference and not a conflict, since an index of national commitments and a test of practice measure different things, and the 2024 index itself lists technical and capacity measures as areas for growth.
gap_reason: The latest EU items, of November 2025 and April 2026, still call for significant strengthening and report major deficiencies, while responses are proposed as adopted on paper (the law, strategy and action plan, the national and government response teams) or only planned (government data centre, secure network, security operations centre), and the disaster recovery centre is used by 3 of about 140 bodies; these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is staffed and trained response teams working to the Reform Agenda standard, security officers and tested plans in institutions, and secure government infrastructure in actual use. The Reform Agenda's 2024 baseline of CERTs not operational sits against statements that MKD-CIRT is in place, possibly because the baseline means NIS2 readiness, and the audit evidence behind this finding is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence, with percentages from a survey of 18 institutions.

label: Security of 5G networks not ensured
priority_reason: Toolbox compliance is a Reform Agenda step and has been named in the Commission's key recommendations in four successive reports, and the enlargement communication presents it as a basis of secure digital infrastructure. The issue is narrow, one clause among several in the chapter's key recommendation, so centrality is the weakest part of this rating and a reviewer could reasonably set Medium. The small number of items did not lower the rating, as volume is not a criterion.
tractability_reason: Few actors are needed, mainly the regulator and the Ministry working with operators, the law already provides the power and by-laws under the 2021 amendments were reported adopted by the following year, which all favour progress. However, not all the 2021 amendments were implemented four years on, a supplier assessment planned from 2023 is not shown as done, and operators complained of having no consultation in 2021. The evidence does not show what restrictions would cost operators, so the rating is not set higher.
direction_reason: The Commission has named the 5G toolbox in its recommendations in four successive reports (2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, two of these items being classified under the framework issue), and its November 2025 wording still asks the country to continue, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Legal steps did occur (2021 amendments, 2022 by-laws, the June 2025 law with supplier risk provisions), but the screening report says not all the 2021 amendments had been implemented. A reviewer could read the 2025 law as the start of improvement, but it began to apply only in June 2026 and no later EU item assesses it.
gap_reason: The latest EU items ask the country to continue implementing the toolbox, including assessing suppliers and restricting high-risk ones, and the Reform Agenda requires the security by-law fully implemented by December 2027; the 2025 law is proposed as adopted, the by-law and supplier assessment as proposed, and the 2021 amendments as reversed because the new law replaces them, all of which are proposals for review. What remains is adopting and applying the by-law and actually carrying out supplier risk assessments and any restrictions, since the law gives the power (machine translated, capped at Medium) but no item shows it used. The Reform Agenda's statement that the step is largely achieved sits against its own partial compliance baseline and the Commission's later wording, and it appears to rest mainly on spectrum and legislation, so it is not treated as closure; the Commission's finding that this law's reform step was not achieved concerns the Code and the Gigabit Act and not the toolbox, and the law allows 15 months for by-laws, so the finding does not decide this gap.

label: Electronic identification and trust services law not aligned
priority_reason: The updated law is a Reform Agenda payment condition, and eIDAS alignment was raised by the Commission in each report from 2022 to 2025. It is the legal base of the electronic identification theme. The rating rests on these requirements and not on the number of items, most of which are provisions of one law.
tractability_reason: The remaining work is mainly legal drafting led by one ministry, with a gap analysis by SIGMA and a by-law roadmap already available, and the ministry met the June 2025 law deadline. Earlier delays in 2022 and 2023 and the staged by-laws, some tied to the wallet in December 2027, are the main limits.
direction_reason: The Commission moved from 'yet to align' (2022) and 'further delayed' (2023) to treating the law as harmonised with the 2014 regulation and asking for the 2024 revision (2024), then to amendments transposing eIDAS 2.0, with 'some progress' for e-government and further efforts required (2025). Sources conflict on whether alignment with the 2014 regulation already existed in 2020 (screening report and 2023 strategy against the 2022 and 2023 reports), which affects the start point but not the trend. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive; the judgement rests on the issue's own items.
gap_reason: The law was amended in June 2025 and the Commission counted the step as achieved for Reform Agenda purposes, while saying the law does not fully align and asking for further efforts in its 2025 report; the intervention statuses used here are themselves proposals. What remains is full alignment of the partially harmonised provisions, adoption of the 14 by-laws, which no item shows as adopted, and actual application. The machine-translated law text, capped at Medium confidence, says the amendments apply only from 1 June 2027.

label: Electronic identification and trust services not usable or recognised
priority_reason: Joining the trusted list and implementing the wallet are Reform Agenda steps, the first with a stated payment provision, and the Commission repeated its concern about the tools in 2024 and 2025. Recognition and use are central to the electronic identification theme.
tractability_reason: The outstanding trusted list tasks are specific and technical, and two providers have passed ministry checks, which favours progress. Use and usability need many institutions and users, the wallet depends on regional partners and the mutual recognition agreement, and the list depends on Commission assessment. The audit found failed procurement of institutional seal certificates (machine translated, capped at Medium), which is a warning on delivery.
direction_reason: The Commission said in 2024 that the tools were cumbersome and neither free nor user friendly, and in 2025 that they were still not, while its 2021 report recorded only a modest rise in electronic signature use. In 2026 it found the trusted list step not achieved despite the request of 30 October 2025, so steps were taken without a changed result. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive, and the 2024 audit evidence that high-level eID did not raise use is machine translated and capped at Medium.
gap_reason: Two providers offer advanced and qualified signature services, as the Commission reports and as the Reform Agenda step asks, but the same step is not achieved, the tools remain not free or user friendly, and the wallet and mutual recognition are still proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. The two sides conflict: North Macedonia reports the trusted list preparation complete and considers the step achieved, while the Commission says the self-assessment and published list are outstanding. What remains is inclusion in the trusted list (grace period to 31 December 2026), usable and free tools in common use, the wallet and cross-border recognition.

label: Interoperability framework not aligned with EU
priority_reason: This is a repeated EU requirement across three reports, but no item places it in a benchmark, a Reform Agenda payment condition or the main findings list of a report. It supports the interoperability theme, yet the Commission itself treats use of the platform as the wider obstacle.
tractability_reason: The mechanism is legal and framework alignment, which one ministry can lead without depending on others. The caution is the record: the recommendation has not moved in three years and the plan is still only stated in a government strategy.
direction_reason: The Commission repeated the recommendation to align with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act in near-identical terms in 2023, 2024 and 2025, which sets the persistent default under the rules. The 2025 wording ('efforts need to continue') reports no result. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive.
gap_reason: The only responding intervention, alignment with the framework, has proposed status at the freeze, and this status is itself a proposal, so no aligned text is shown. Items are in tension and this is not recorded in the contradictions file: the 2023 screening says the framework is aligned with framework 2.0, while the 2023 report asks for alignment with the 2017 revision and the audit (machine translated, capped at Medium) found no study confirming alignment. What remains is a national framework shown to be aligned with the current European framework and with the Interoperable Europe Act.

label: Interoperability platform and data exchange underused
priority_reason: Data exchange and ex officio evidence sit in a Reform Agenda payment condition, and completing data exchange is a repeated recommendation on public administration reform in 2023, 2024 and 2025, in the main findings in the last two. It is central to the interoperability and data themes. The large number of items, mostly from one national audit, played no part in this rating.
tractability_reason: The platform exists and the government controls it, and use has risen somewhat, which favours progress. Against that, the audit found about 1,300 obliged institutions with no costed plan, IT pay at less than half the private sector and no coordinating body, findings the 2025 strategy partly repeats (all machine translated, capped at Medium), and the Commission cites missing software and lack of will. ITU's account of a ministers' council is a noted difference over a different body, leaving how far coordination worked in practice uncertain.
direction_reason: Commission wording that few institutions use the platform runs from 2020 through 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, which sets the persistent default; the 2025 report records only efforts and repeats the requirement. Connection and transaction figures rose (39 institutions in 2021 to 58 or 63 in 2025; 1.5 million transactions in 2022 to 8 million in 2024), and the Commission confirms the increases in 2023 and 2024, but the counts come from government documents, machine translated and capped at Medium, and most institutions remain outside. The 2020 Commission 'slight increase' and the audit's falling traffic are a noted difference of measure and period, and the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.
gap_reason: The platform operates and some institutions, such as customs, exchange data regularly, but the 2025 Commission recommendation still asks to complete data exchange and the responding upgrades and reforms are mainly proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. There is a confirmed contradiction: the country told the 2023 screening that the once-only principle is applied, while its 2024 Reform Agenda says institutions still do not gather evidence ex officio. What remains is regular use of the platform by the institutions obliged to use it, so that evidence is obtained ex officio as the law prescribes.

label: Customs IT systems not aligned with EU electronic customs
priority_reason: E-customs steps appear in the Reform Agenda with a stated payment provision for Phase 6, and the customs IT recommendation recurs from 2021 to 2025, in the main findings in 2024 and 2025. The Commission calls alignment on accession critical to EU financial interests and security, so the issue is central to Chapter 29. Some Reform Agenda items carry a theme_doubtful flag because their wording stresses efficiency, not connection to the EU.
tractability_reason: One capable agency leads, and it has delivered NCTS Phase 5 after delay and kept Phase 4 running satisfactorily. The limits are IT staffing, the planned 15 experts not yet shown as hired, cost, and an EU-driven timetable to 2030.
direction_reason: NCTS Phase 5 preparation started by 2021, delays were reported in 2023 and 2024, and the system launched in January 2025, with the Commission noting 'good progress' on IT systems in 2025. The Commission's recommendation to consolidate systems repeats each year, but the stated result changed. The sub-area wording matches this issue, yet the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.
gap_reason: NCTS Phase 5 is live, but the 2025 screening rates alignment between low and partial, and Phase 6, the export system and ICS2 are proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is development of the remaining systems under the strategic plan, costed at about EUR 34.5 million, with full alignment planned for 2026 to 2030.

label: Not ready for EU justice, home affairs and border information systems
priority_reason: The systems matter for Chapter 24, but support is thin: one screening report states the requirements and no item shows a benchmark, Reform Agenda condition or repeated key recommendation. This is central with thin support.
tractability_reason: Progress depends on the EU: the Commission says EU law gives candidates no Eurodac access, and the country reports it cannot build to Eurodac without the technical specifications and struggles to secure funding. The Frontex plan offers a route for border systems, but no item shows it being carried out.
direction_reason: The requirements on ECRIS, the Visa Information System and Eurodac come essentially from one 2023 screening report, so there is no repeated or changed wording to compare. The 2021, 2022 and 2024 items concern a Frontex biometric plan and do not show whether readiness moved. The chapter scale was context only and not decisive.
gap_reason: Responding interventions are proposed or lack a clear status, and these statuses are themselves proposals; part of the requirement falls due only at accession, and Eurodac access before accession has no legal basis, so 'open' does not by itself mean late. What remains is a functional criminal records system with ECRIS analysis done, the technical adaptations for the Visa Information System, an IT structure compatible with Eurodac on accession, and the funding for them.

label: Not ready to connect to other EU sectoral information systems
priority_reason: Each requirement is repeated, and tax interoperability reaches the main findings in 2024 and 2025 and CECIS is an issue for immediate attention in 2024, but none is central to the theme as a whole and the only Reform Agenda references are railway and freight outputs in the government's text. This is a residual group spanning several chapters, so the rating is an average that would differ by sector.
tractability_reason: The sectors differ: food safety shows active use of EU tools, the CECIS link looks technically limited yet has not been finished in over five years, and BRIS requires full company law alignment and access to groups open only to Member States and EEA countries. The rating is a mid-point, not a uniform finding.
direction_reason: The sectors do not share one trend, so this rests on those with repeated wording: CECIS from 2020 to 2025 (with 'no progress' in 2023), the business registers link from 2023 to 2025, and EU tax systems and own resources in 2024 and 2025.
